title: Strait of Hormuz: The 33 km Gap a Fifth of the World's Oil Must Cross

minor: Albuquerque reached Hormuz in 1507 but did not take it then; 'arrived' is accurate, though the line could add that he withdrew before returning in 1515.
'Two countries face the strait: Iran to the north, Oman to the south' ignores the UAE coast just west of Musandam; 'the narrows' would be safer wording.

'Most Saudi and Emirati oil leaves this way too' has no source entry. The EIA only supports that Saudi Arabia sends the most crude through Hormuz. Both countries also have bypass routes. Say 'much of' or add a source.
'As many analysts put it' in the outro is an unattributed appeal to authority; attribute it or make it the script's own line.
'Iran's case, made by its officials for decades' has no sources entry.
'The first empire that treated this gap as a gate' is arguable, since the Hormuz kingdom taxed trade here before Portugal. 'The first European empire' is safer.
'Asia would be most exposed' is an inference from the EIA's 69%/84% figures, not an EIA statement.

shots.vo: Every day, about 20 million barrels of oil pass through the Strait of Hormuz.
At its narrowest, the US government measures it at 21 miles: about 33 kilometres.
About a fifth of all the oil the world uses.

document.title: US EIA, 'Amid regional conflict, the Strait of Hormuz remains critical oil chokepoint', 16 June 2025
document.highlight: Oil flow through the strait averaged 20 million barrels per day in 2024, the equivalent of about 20% of global petroleum liquids consumption.

shots.vo: Tension around here has moved crude prices before.
Most of it sails to China, India, Japan and South Korea.

stat.label: share of Hormuz crude going to China, India, Japan and South Korea, 2024 (EIA)

shots.vo: Two countries face the strait: Iran to the north, Oman to the south.
How did 33 kilometres of sea get this grip? It starts in 1507.

shots.vo: Behind the strait lies the Gulf: about 990 kilometres long, and shallow, rarely deeper than 90 metres.
Kuwait, Iraq, Bahrain and Qatar have no other sea route. Most Saudi and Emirati oil leaves this way too.
By the EIA's count, Saudi Arabia sends more crude through Hormuz than any other country.
On the northern shore sit Iran's port of Bandar Abbas and a curtain of islands: Qeshm, Hormuz and Larak.
On the southern shore is Musandam, a rocky tip of Oman, cut off from the rest of the country by the United Arab Emirates.
How wide is the gap? The EIA says 21 miles, about 33 kilometres; Encyclopaedia Britannica gives 55 to 95, depending which shores are measured.
Ships use only part of it: one lane in, one lane out, each two miles wide, with a two-mile buffer between.
Two miles each way, for a fifth of the world's oil.

stat.label: width of each shipping lane through Hormuz (EIA)

shots.vo: Under the law of the sea, every coast may claim 12 nautical miles of territorial sea.
Here the two claims overlap. There is no open sea in the narrows, and the lanes run through Oman's waters.
It is not only oil. About a fifth of the world's trade in liquefied gas passes too, most of it from Qatar.
Qatar's North Field is the same gas reservoir that Iran, across the water, calls South Pars.
Then most cargoes turn east. In 2024, the EIA counted 84 per cent of the crude through Hormuz heading to Asian markets.
A few pipelines avoid the strait. The EIA estimates their unused room at about 2.6 million barrels a day.
Set beside the 20 million that pass by sea, that is a side door, not a second gate.
And inside the Gulf, near the shipping lanes, sit three small islands whose owner is still disputed.
To see why, go back to the first empire that treated this gap as a gate.

shots.vo: In 1507, the island of Hormuz was the seat of a rich trading kingdom, taxing goods between India, Persia and Arabia.
That year a Portuguese fleet under Afonso de Albuquerque arrived, having sailed round Africa.
He returned in 1515, took the island for good and raised a fortress. Its walls still stand.
From Hormuz and Goa, Portugal sold passes called cartazes, and ships trading in the waters it claimed were expected to carry one.
For more than a century, the gate answered to a fleet from the far side of the world.
In 1622, Persia's Shah Abbas the First took Hormuz, with ships of the English East India Company fighting on his side.
Trade moved to the mainland, to the port that still carries his name: Bandar Abbas. The northern shore became Persian, and it has stayed Persian in sovereignty.
To the south, Britain signed treaties in 1820 and 1853 with the sheikhdoms of the coast, which came to be called the Trucial States.
In January 1968, the British government announced it would withdraw its forces from the Gulf by the end of 1971.

headline.text: Britain to pull its forces out of the Gulf by the end of 1971

shots.vo: On 30 November 1971, as Britain left, Iranian forces landed on Abu Musa and on the Greater and Lesser Tunb.
Abu Musa was covered by an agreement with Sharjah, signed that month, which each side reads differently. The Tunbs, claimed by Ras al-Khaimah, were not.
Two days later, the United Arab Emirates was formed. It has claimed all three islands ever since.
Iran says the islands are Iranian and not up for talks; the UAE calls them occupied and seeks talks or the world court. So the line is drawn twice.

map.label: Claimed by Iran and the UAE

shots.vo: Then came war. From 1984, Iraq and Iran attacked each other's oil shipping, and soon the tankers of other countries.
In 1987, the United States put Kuwaiti tankers under the American flag and escorted them from the strait to Kuwait.
In April 1988, after a mine damaged a US frigate, the US Navy struck Iranian oil platforms and ships.

headline.text: US Navy hits Iranian platforms and ships after mine damages frigate

shots.vo: In 1995, the US Navy re-formed its Fifth Fleet, based in Bahrain. The US Navy now kept a standing fleet inside the gate, which Iran calls a threat and the US calls protection.
Portugal, Persia, Britain, America: each drew a line here, by force or by treaty. In 1982, lawyers tried to draw one for everyone.

shots.vo: The UN Convention on the Law of the Sea, signed in December 1982, created a right for straits like this one: transit passage.

document.title: United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea, 10 December 1982, Article 38
document.highlight: all ships and aircraft enjoy the right of transit passage, which shall not be impeded

shots.vo: Under it, ships may cross a strait's territorial waters without asking, and the states on its shores may not stop them.
Iran signed in 1982 but has never ratified. On signing, it declared that such rights belong only to states that join the treaty.
The United States has not joined the convention either. It says transit passage is customary law, binding on every state.
Oman ratified in 1989, and the lanes run through Omani water. So the same narrows are read under two legal maps.
Along the northern shore, from Bandar Abbas to the islands, are bases of Iran's navy and of the Revolutionary Guards' navy.
Iran's case, made by its officials for decades: the Gulf's security belongs to the countries around it, and foreign fleets bring tension, not safety.
In 2019, President Hassan Rouhani took that case to the UN, proposing a pact of the Gulf states he called the Hormuz Peace Endeavour.
When sanctions targeted its oil, Iranian officials warned more than once that the strait could close. In 2011, a vice-president said not a drop would pass.

headline.text: Iran's vice-president warns no oil will pass Hormuz if its exports are sanctioned

shots.vo: In July 2019, British Royal Marines helped Gibraltar detain the Iranian tanker Grace 1, suspected of carrying oil to Syria against EU sanctions.
Fifteen days later, the Revolutionary Guards seized the British-flagged Stena Impero in the strait. Iran cited maritime violations; Britain called the seizure illegal.
Earlier in 2019, tankers were damaged off Fujairah and in the Gulf of Oman. The United States blamed Iran; Iran denied it.
In April 2024, the Guards seized the container ship MSC Aries near the strait.
In June 2025, Iran's parliament backed closing the strait. The final word lay with its security council, and the strait stayed open.

headline.text: Iran's parliament backs closing Hormuz; final decision left to security council

shots.vo: The other side's case, put by the US and Gulf Arab states: a route carrying a fifth of the world's oil cannot depend on one country's consent.
In 2019, the US and partners formed a naval mission, based in Bahrain, to watch and accompany ships through the strait.
Saudi Arabia built a way round: the East-West pipeline, about 1,200 kilometres from its Gulf oilfields to Yanbu on the Red Sea, rated at 5 million barrels a day.
The UAE's line from Habshan to Fujairah, outside the strait, can carry 1.5 million barrels a day.
Iran built its own. In July 2021 it loaded its first cargo at Jask, beyond the strait, from a new pipeline.
And Oman keeps talking to both: in April 2025 it hosted US-Iran talks in Muscat. So what would actually move this map?
Scenario one: the strait is blocked, even for days. Despite many warnings, Iran has never closed it, not even during the Tanker War.
On the EIA's numbers, with every spare pipeline full, about 17 million barrels a day would still have no other way out.

stat.label: barrels a day with no pipeline route, on EIA 2024 figures

shots.vo: If it closed, Asia would be most exposed: the EIA counts 69 per cent of the strait's crude going to China, India, Japan and South Korea.
Importing members of the International Energy Agency must hold oil stocks equal to at least 90 days of net imports.
Scenario two: more pipes. Iraq and Jordan agreed in 2013 on a pipeline from Basra to Aqaba. More than a decade on, it has not been built.
Saudi Arabia has shown its line can stretch: in 2019 it converted gas-liquids pipes and temporarily raised East-West capacity to 7 million barrels a day.
But every pipe ends on another sea. Oil loaded at Yanbu for Asia must still pass Bab el-Mandeb, another narrow strait.
Gas runs the other way. QatarEnergy plans to raise LNG output from 77 to 142 million tonnes a year by about 2030, all shipped through Hormuz.
Scenario three: the world needs less of what passes here. In 2023, the International Energy Agency projected oil demand peaking before 2030 under current policies.

headline.text: IEA projects demand for oil, gas and coal peaking before 2030

shots.vo: OPEC disagrees. Its 2024 outlook has demand still rising, to about 120 million barrels a day in 2050.

stat.label: OPEC's projection of world oil demand in 2050 (World Oil Outlook 2024)

shots.vo: If the IEA is right, traffic through this gap slowly thins. If OPEC is right, the gap matters more each year.
So it isn't 33 kilometres of water that control a fifth of the world's oil. It is, as many analysts put it, an agreement renewed every day to leave them open.
The next gate sits at the other end of Arabia: Bab el-Mandeb, 18 miles wide by the EIA's count.
Since late 2023, attacks on shipping there have sent many ships the long way round Africa.
